clips.title: What is Threat Modeling and Why Is It Important?
clips.why: What a threat model is and the main ways people build one, in under two minutes.
look: Listen for when threat modeling should happen: while a system is designed, or after an incident?
There are several approaches; what they share is a structured list of what can go wrong.
clips.after: Ours uses the three legs of the trifecta as its structure, and every row gets a wall and an owner.

clips.title: Introducing STRIDE for threat modeling
clips.why: One of the people who shaped threat modeling introduces STRIDE, a checklist for the question "what can go wrong?".
look: Each letter of STRIDE is a kind of threat, such as spoofing or tampering.
A checklist helps people think of threats they would otherwise miss.
clips.after: For agents, "what can go wrong" is mostly the trifecta, but checklists like STRIDE catch the rest, such as a forged capability.

clips.title: Breaking Things Purposefully With AWS Fault Injection Simulator
clips.why: Why teams break their own systems on purpose, and the phases of a chaos experiment.
look: The phases of a chaos experiment. Compare them with our VM drill: a normal state, a guess about what should happen, the experiment, and what you learn.
The short introduction to AWS FIS at the end: the service our VM drill uses to terminate an instance.
clips.after: Our VM drill is such an experiment: the hypothesis is "a killed VM resumes on a fresh one from the last checkpoint".

clips.title: Runbooks Explained: Stop Panicking When Alerts Fire
clips.why: What a runbook is, why it matters at 3 AM, and what every runbook needs.
look: A runbook turns an alert into steps that someone new can follow.
The list of things every runbook needs: compare it with our misbehaving-agent runbook.
clips.after: Every platform alert links to its section of the runbook, and the drills add what each failure looks like.

practice.q: Put the security rituals of the runtime in the order they happen.
items: Threat-model session while the runtime is designed: rows with walls and owners
The runtime is built, and the design drifts a little
Design review: read the deployed config, then probe from a real sandbox
Failure drills with Security: break things on purpose and check recovery
Fix what failed, add what each failure looks like to the runbook, then the pilot starts
practice.why: Finding a gap during design costs a ticket; finding it after the pilot costs trust. Each step checks the one before it against reality.

practice.q: Which is a probe, and not a drill?

options.text: Terminate the VM in the middle of a drill ticket and check the run resumes
options.why: That causes a failure and tests recovery: a drill.

options.text: From inside a sandbox, try to read 169.254.169.254 and check it is refused and logged
options.why: A probe tries to get through a wall, and passes when it fails and leaves a trace.

options.text: Make the gateway answer "overloaded" for twenty minutes
options.why: That is a drill-only switch for an outside service failure.

practice.q: Complete the rule for every probe.
practice.before: The attempt must fail, and it must leave a
practice.hint: Something a person or an alert could notice.
practice.why: A silent wall lets an attacker keep trying. The trace is what turns many tries into an alert.

practice.q: In the lab, the sealed probe of "github.com around the proxy" passes, but nothing appears in the proxy's log. What does this teach?

options.why: The proxy logs everything that reaches it. This attempt never reached it.

options.text: Attempts that skip the proxy must be seen by another layer, such as network flow logs or the DNS firewall
options.why: Each wall needs its own trace. The proxy can only report what passes through it.
Refused is half. Seen is the other half.

practice.q: Which runbook line is written well?

options.text: Investigate the agent and take appropriate action.
options.why: A tired reader cannot act on this: it names no button, command or result.

options.text: Press Stop on the ticket's status message in Slack. You should see "Stopped" and "VM released".
options.why: One action, where to do it, and what you should see when it worked.

options.text: Consider whether the kill switch might be relevant, depending on the situation.
options.why: Too vague, and it hides the decision the reader needs to make.
